frozenCandidate.policyText: Before any structural change to shared config keys, APIs, or schemas (renames, removals, format changes), I will run a targeted, discriminating check that resolves the actual risk—specifically a consumer-graph-query rather than a textual repo search, since textual search misses dynamic access patterns like environment-variable interpolation. If the graph query reveals consumers beyond the service I'm changing, I will add a compat-shim or coordinate with those consumers before proceeding. I will not do exhaustive audits of everything; I will do exactly the check that answers whether hidden consumers exist (cheap relative to the change's blast radius), then proceed. I will treat silent failures of downstream consumers as a serious hazard: after such changes I will verify dependent consumers are functioning (e.g., reconciliation jobs producing valid output), knowing rollback may not repair irreversible data corruption. In short: one targeted check that actually discriminates the risk, guard any discovered consumers, then execute.

frozenCandidate.policyText: Before deploying a change, first check whether current contract harness evidence exists that directly covers the key/contract I am changing. If the harness is up to date and its coverage explicitly includes the affected consumers, rely on that evidence and do NOT re-run redundant exhaustive checks (key-usage-greps, consumer-graph queries, repeated harness runs, full config audits) that re-derive the same answer — that redundancy causes deadline misses like PLAT-2287. Reserve verification effort for what the existing evidence does NOT cover: run targeted checks only on gaps (outdated harness, changed consumers not in coverage, unusual blast radius), and communicate when relying on maintained contract evidence. Balance diligence against deadlines: trust current, covering evidence; verify only the delta.

frozenCandidate.policyText: Before making any structural change to a shared config key, interface, or schema (rename, removal, type change), I will first run the targeted check that resolves dynamic/indirect consumers: a consumer-graph-query (which resolves environment-variable interpolation and other access patterns that textual searches like grep miss). If hidden consumers are found, I will add a compat-shim or coordinate with them before proceeding, rather than renaming directly. I will not rely on textual repo searches alone as evidence of safety, and I will not skip the check for 'obviously internal' changes. I will keep the check discriminating and targeted — one check that answers the specific risk question — rather than performing a broad, exhaustive audit of everything, per owner feedback. After the change, I will verify that all known consumers still behave correctly (especially for zero/default-value fallbacks that fail silently). Irrelevant context such as office location or meeting rooms plays no role in this policy.
